title: How (and Why) to Use Humor in the Classroom
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart makes the case that humor is a key ingredient of great teaching even for teachers who, like him, often watch jokes land with awkward silence. He opens with Daniel Coyle's line that laughter signals safety and connection, then cites David Sousa on the physiological benefits and Daniela Jeder on cognitive ones such as sustaining attention and arousing curiosity. He ties humor to his five key beliefs, saying it shows competence, builds belonging and dampens hostility that can derail classroom management. Joy is the last benefit: laughter makes mutual delight more frequent when people tackle hard things together. He argues humor is a learnable skill and lists five ways to improve it, including a unicorn-drawing extra-credit joke, before ending with a warning about sarcasm and a promise to say more next time.
points: Stuart roots the case for humor in safety and connection, quoting Daniel Coyle, and then supports it with Sousa's physiological and Jeder's cognitive findings.
He ties humor to credibility, belonging and caring, so it becomes a motivation tool and not a mere nicety.
He names joy as the fundamental payoff, since laughter increases moments of mutual joy while learning something hard.
He insists humor is learnable and offers five specific steps, including books, a video on content and delivery, and the unicorn bit.
He closes with a warning that classroom humor research cautions against certain forms, particularly sarcasm, and asks whether sarcasm is really fine if everyone gets it.
quotes: Have you ever had one of those awkward moments where you tell your students a joke or share with them something that you think is funny, only to have them stare at you like you're dumb?

When we're capably humorous (as I confessed, I'm still working on this), it demonstrates a form of competence to our kids. Competence is one of the Cs in the CCP of credibility. It shows the students, “Hey, this person knows stuff. She is good at things.

When people laugh together, it enhances their sense of belonging with the group. This sense of belonging makes it easier for our students to align their identities with the kind of work we ask them to do in the classroom.
Humor dampens hostility and aggression — two things that can very quickly blow up your classroom management plan or mess up these senses in your students that you Care (the other C in CCP).

And there's one last thing: joy. Laughter cultivates the joy that should come when we're with other people doing something good. And every day that we get to be in a class with our kids and try to learn something that's tough — that's a beautiful thing. That's a situation where joy can live. Laughter helps increase the frequency of those moments of mutual joy in the classroom.

When kids ask on a quiz if they can get extra credit for doing something extra, say, “No, but you can get a unicorn.” And then actually have some kid draw unicorns on the papers of the kids who do the extra thing.

All the literature on humor in the classroom warns against certain kinds of humor, particularly sarcasm. Now if you're like a good chunk of my smart, witty readership, that probably makes you think, “Dave, c'mon now — sarcasm is fine as long as everyone gets it.” Is it, though?
